newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels target key southern mining capital.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels target key southern mining capital.

text.p: Rebels, flush from their biggest victory yet in Zaire's third city Kisangani, said on Sunday they were aiming next for the southern mining hub of Lubumbashi but added that targets included the capital Kinshasa.
The rebels, who took up arms in October vowing to topple veteran and ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko, swept into Kisangani on Saturday after soldiers looted what they could and fled.

"Lubumbashi is the next big target...but all the towns of the republic are targets including Kinshasa itself," rebel information chief Raphael Ghenda told journalists in the eastern border town of Goma.
Lubumbashi, Zaire's second largest city, is the capital of Shaba region and has long been a centre for opposition to Mobutu, who has ruled since seizing power in 1965.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila told a news conference in Goma on Saturday that there could be no ceasefire before negotiations, adding that these should be with Mobutu himself.
"We are still advancing, we must liberate the whole country," he said, adding that talks with Mobutu "may constitute some kind of pause".
Ghenda said Kabila was expected to visit Kisangani, the former nerve centre of army operations in the war zone and base for a failed January 20 government counter-offensive, on Sunday.
The Tutsi-led rebels now control about one fifth of the sprawling Central African nation.
Mobutu, 66, has rarely visited his country since undergoing prostate cancer surgery in Europe in August. He is currently in the south of France.
The copper and cobalt produced in Shaba, like the diamonds of neighbouring Kasai, are vital to government control of the national economy.

Ghenda confirmed reports on rebel radio that the lakeside town of Pweto, 400 km (250 miles) northeast of Lubumbashi, had fallen to the rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL). "Pweto fell two days ago and the forces have gone even further, beyond Pweto," he said.

Regional military sources said rebels took Pweto with little fighting as undisciplined government forces, demoralised by reports of rebel advances and anger from local residents, put up little resistance.
The rebels took up arms accusing the Zairean authorities of denying them citizenship and preparing to expel them to Rwanda, their ancestral home.
They seized Uvira in South Kivu last October, moved north to take Goma in November and Bunia in December before fanning west to attack Kisangani from several directions.
At the same time the advance headed south into Shaba, seizing control of a string of towns including Kalemie and Moba.
The rebel advance has uprooted hundreds of thousands of Rwandan Hutus who fled to Zaire fearing reprisals after the 1994 genocide in Rwanda by Hutu radicals of minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus.

Up to 700,000 opted to return to Rwanda in December when their camps near the border in the east came under rebel attack. Armed Hutu radicals and several hundred thousand Hutu refugees fled west and are trapped in the war zone.
The Zaire government has accepted a U.N. ceasefire plan. Kabila had talks on Saturday with U.N. envoy Mohamed Sahnoun.
